utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and outside listening and watching our procedure. I see you on your feet, Mr. Gajic. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'd like to greet everyone. And today I'd especially like to greet Judge Nyambe and the representatives of the Registrar to congratulate them on Women's Day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are all in the majority in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: We are aware about that. [Interpretation] Defence would like to respond to a part of the Prosecution's request submitted on the 22nd of February, 2010, which has to do with Witness 187. He was foreseen to testify towards the end of the month. By your leave, we'd like to put forth our arguments concerning this Prosecution's motion. Namely, first I need to stress that it is a rather unusual request, in particular if we have in mind the procedural history of Prosecution motions and Chamber decisions regarding Witness 187. Namely, Prosecution as early as the 18th of March, 2009, submitted their request to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, which inter alia included their request for Witness 187 to testify in accordance with the Rule 92 ter. The Defence on the 24th of July, 2009, submitted its response to the 92 ter request by the OTP in which we objected their request concerning Witness 187, pointing out, among other things, the nature of General Obradovic's testimony, that is, the testimony of Witness 187. We also stated that Witness 187 in the Popovic case testified as a Defence witness. Also, General Obradovic witnessed and was supposed to testify the acts and conduct of General Tolimir which may serve as a basis to put forth his evidence based on Rule 92 ter. We also touched upon the cross-examination of the OTP briefly as conducted by Mr. McCloskey in the Popovic case. Next, on the 30th of July, 2009, the Prosecution submitted a motion to reply to our response pursuant to their 92 ter request. In paragraph 2 of the reply, the Prosecution states that following their analysis of our response, they withdrew their request concerning Witness 187, and they expressed their wish to hear the witness viva voce and in totality. By virtue of the Chamber's decision of the 3rd of November, 2009, the request of the OTP was approved to withdraw their 92 ter request concerning Witness 187. To put it simply, we are now in a situation in which in the latest Prosecution motion we have their request following the granting of their wish to withdraw Witness 187 initially, as granted by the Chamber. In addition to these arguments, I'd also like to state that according to the schedule disclosed by the Prosecution this witness was supposed to testify in the last week of the month of March 2011. This witness in the Popovic case testified for three days. And without related documentary evidence, his transcript amounted to -- his testimony amounted to 287 pages of the transcript. As we all know, preparing for such a witness is very demanding and preparing for a 92 ter witness puts a much greater burden and effort than when we hear a witness viva voce. I also wanted to say that in their request of the 28th of November, 2008, the OTP requested that this witness be put on their list of witnesses, assessing that his direct examination would last for three hours. In our view, this is reasonable given the numerous topics this witness is supposed to address. The Prosecution announced that the witness was supposed to testify inter alia about the organisational structure of the Main Staff of the VRS, the position of General Tolimir and his role in Srebrenica and Zepa, next on the issue of humanitarian convoys, and some others which I won't go into at this moment. It is for all these reasons that the Defence object the request put forth by the Prosecution concerning Witness 187. We propose to the Chamber that the request of the 28th of February, 2010, concerning this witness be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. Does the Prosecution want to respond to this submission? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour, Mr. President, Your Honours. No, I think that enough has been said. We're ready to go with however the Court wishes on this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take into consideration the arguments of both parties, and we'll render a decision as soon as possible. Thank you very much. Before the witness is being brought in, I have to express my apologies to Mr. Vanderpuye. You were right with your time estimation for the current witness of one hour and 30 minutes. It was a communication problem in the Chamber. And, of course, you may use your time you have indicated earlier. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- Dr. Barr. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Vanderpuye is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Dr. Barr.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have, please, 65 ter 7212 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's loading, let me just tell you that -- well, I think it's here already. This is your 8th January, 2010, report concerning typewritten documents, and I wondered if you could just briefly outline the difference, if there is any, between analysing a typewritten document and analysing a handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same basic principle would apply in that, again, it's a like-for-like comparison, so the process in effect would start the same. You would literally go through the typewritten document, examining each character to determine how it's been constructed. The difference is you would be looking -- obviously on a typewritten document you won't get the range of variation because typescript's fixed, but what you would be doing is looking for how it's been produced and whether there are any defects that would enable you to identify that specific machine as opposed to any other machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you use any specific or special devices in order to conduct the examination in this case?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it's really a case of using a microscope so that you can see the detail of the typescript more closely than you could just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to page number 3, and it should be item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have the instructions that you received, if you're able to see that on the screen, maybe not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, you do have the report in front of you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Here you've indicated that you received a certain number of -- a certain number of documents. It appears to be four documents. One is a typewritten document dated 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the record that's P125. I do have the original here if the Court would like to inspect it or see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then you received three other documents. And with respect to any of these documents, were you provided any other -- any additional information concerning the machine that produced it or anything of that nature that might identify -- might identify the typewriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just provided with those four documents and asked if they'd all been produced on the same machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having examined these documents can you tell us what kind of machine it was produced by or these documents were produced by?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appearance of the typescript is such that they appear to have been produced by an old-fashioned manual typewriter rather than a more modern word process document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly how you can tell the difference between, for example, a modern printer or relatively modern printer that uses the same kind of casing that you see on a typewriter and a typewriter itself?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a case of looking at -- these have all been produced with a fabric ribbon, which, again, you tend -- you only see on the older document -- older type of typewriters rather than a word process document. And the appearance of the typescript is an old-fashioned style of font.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to -- just so that we're clear, which of these four documents was the questioned document as it were, and which ones were the ones that were used for comparison purposes if -- or were they all simply -- were you asked to compare all four of them?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, my instructions were to say had they all been produced on one machine. So it wasn't a case of taking -- saying, these are specimens, have -- has this been produced on the same machine that produces these other documents; it was literally, have all these four been produced on one machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, and that will be item number -- oops, I'm sorry, I should have gone to item number 6. Yeah, we have it. In making these comparisons, you concluded in summary form that there was a conclusive evidence that document 0425-8580, which is P125, and document 0441-0981, that there was conclusive evidence that they were produced by the same machine. And can you tell us how you arrived at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These two documents were produced -- the typestyle of the printing was the same. And the spacing of the document, the number of characters you get in a specific length, was the same. So that indicated they were both produced on the same type of machine. And then to be able to say that it's conclusively that one machine, what you're doing is looking for defects that will uniquely identify one machine as opposed to other machines produced in the same fashion. With these two, what I found was that there was damage to the lower-case P. The lower-case V tended to print more darkly on these characters. And also there was a red colour associated with the bottom part of the characters. I think old-style machines quite often had two colour ribbons; you'd got black at one -- at the top, red at the bottom. So it looked as though that was slightly out of alignment so that the characters were typing across the boundary between the grey and the black -- the grey and the red, sorry. So the combination of those three factors were, in my opinion, enough to say that this was -- they were produced on this one specific machine rather than two different machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of things. First, were you provided with originals of these documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the second question is: The observations that you've made particularly concerning the ribbon or the colouration associated with the characters that are printed on the page, are you able to make those observations, you know, with the naked eye, as opposed to using a microscope?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more obvious with a microscope. They were printing very palely so you might have got an indication, but it's more obvious with a microscope.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First I'd like to show the Trial Chamber, really, P125. If we could have that in e-court for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness in the meantime. On page 7, line 23 and 24, you first said, "the characters were typing across the boundary between the grey and the black," and then you corrected yourself, "the grey and ... red, sorry." Are you really referring to grey and red?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, grey simply because I think it was an old ribbon so it was actually typing more grey than black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only, and only, the B/C/S because I'd like to place side by side with this document P517. Mr. President, I should let you know I also have the originals of this documents if it would assist the Court, and I can provide them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, on the right of this -- of the screen in e-court now we have a document that's indicating that it's from the IKM of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. It indicates Borike at 1400 hours. And this is a document that is sent to the commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska and concerns, among other things, 1.000 members of the 28th Division of the BiH Army captured in the area of Dushanovo Kasaba. This document, according to your report, was produced by the same printer as the document on the left. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same typewriter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The same typewriter. And you did that based upon a comparison of the characters. Was there any character in particular that you identified as conclusive?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's taking it as its totality, but as I said, in this case there is damage to the lower-case P, the same damage in the lower-case P to both of them. Again, the V tends to print more darkly. These were printing quite pale at the bottom, but the V was quite dark at the bottom and also got the same mix of colours, grey and red, in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I want to show -- well let me just ask you this. In your conclusion, and I won't put that up just now, but in the conclusion of your report, you say that in your opinion that there's certain similarities also that there's strong evidence between a document 0441-0992, that it was produced by the same machine as the machine that produced these two documents on the screen. What I'd like to do is to ask you about that one, and I'll put it up in just a minute. But do you recall what the basis of that conclusion was?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Again, the same basic style and spacing was the same on this third document. It also had the same damage to the P. The difference was, in this time, the red colouration was coming out at the top of the characters rather on the bottom of the characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just replace P517 with P518 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Vanderpuye kindly speak into the microphone or turn on the other microphone as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have the document 0441-0992 that's referred to in your report at paragraph 6.2 which, in your opinion, shows strong evidence of being produced by the same typewriter as the document on the right, which is P125. Now, was there anything other than what you've indicated previously that ties these two documents together?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the damage features to the P and V, no. You've still got the same difference in that they were printing in two colours. It was just that it was -- the orientation was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would that suggest that it was just printed with a different ribbon or that it was printed with a different machine?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Printed with a different ribbon or that the position of the ribbon had been moved between the printing of the previous documents and this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you the last document, which is 0441-0972. Let me get you the P numbers. P520.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your report at paragraph 6.3, you opine that the document -- that that particular document, that there's conclusive evidence that it was typed on a different machine compared to the other three documents.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the one that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be coming up in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen or we have a problem with a number again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- this one's marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- 971. The one I was referring to was 972.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. We don't have it? Okay. I think we have the original though. If we could perhaps show this to the witness or have that placed on the ELMO, that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem with that, but I wonder if there is a possibility to call up P972.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'm told it's on page 2. There's the magic. Okay. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is the document that you excluded as being produced by the same machine as -- well, the document on the right has now disappeared. Produced on the same machine as P125, which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is again on the screen on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In a blink of an eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've excluded these two from being a match so to speak?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And on what basis did you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The capital M on the document 972, the middle of the document is higher in this typescript than it is in the others, so it's a different M that's on the machine. On top of which, this machine, a number of the characters are filled in which is often an indication of dirt on the type-slug, so you've got dirt and you've also got a different character on there which would indicate that it was a different machine, because on the old-style machines, the character is fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. May there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine. And may all the present ladies have a nice Women's Day, including the witness. Can Mr. Vanderpuye clarify the following: The two documents that we see on our screens, were they produced on the same typewriter? It was rather confusing to me. I didn't ultimately understand whether they do originate from the same typewriter. I mean D72 and 58 -- or, rather, I'm referring to the last three digits of the ERN numbers, 972 and 580, do they come from the same machine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the witness has answered that, but I'm sure she'd be happy to answer it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They come from different machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness now 65 ter 7212A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, Dr. Barr, do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was images that I produced as part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And specifically, the references that you made to the damage to the P, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us where it is, just so that we have an idea.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can see the P in the upper left-hand box, there is actually a yellow arrow, it doesn't come out very well, indicating that the serif on the bottom left-hand side, there, is damaged, it's not printing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And if we can take a look at the O now. Is this the reference that you made to the red printing - it doesn't appear so red on the screen - but is this --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the originals of those which would show it more clearly if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next page, please. Just for the record, this refers to -- this frame of photos refers to document 0425-8580, which is P125. The next is 0441-0972, which was P520, which we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what we have here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's an illustration. The lower frame shows that the P is undamaged, which again goes to my opinion that it was a different machine. It also shows what we've called in-fill on the A, the normal course of that is when you get dirt on the typewriter, the characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please. Here we have document 044981, which was P517.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- this was a document that you opined had strong evidence that was produced by the same machine as produced P125, and can you tell us about what we have here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it was conclusive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Conclusive evidence. That's right. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you can see that the damage to the P in the upper left frame, the red colouration at the bottom of the O, and the fact that the V prints more darkly than the other characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to show you the last one, which refers to document number 0441-0992, and that's P518. And tell us about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This was the document for which you found there was strong evidence that it was printed by the same typewriter as P125?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the P on the upper left, you can see there is damage to the serif. It looks slightly different in this one simply because you're getting the paler red at the top. The dark is printing, so you can actually see the damage more clearly. And it does contrast quite strongly with the document that I excluded, where the serif was horizontal. You've got the red colouration at the top of the characters, but again you've got a dark-printing V.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I just wanted to show you, last, the page which contains the letter M that you compared across all the documents, and that's -- should be two pages up, ERN ending 363. Okay. And here we can see the document that you excluded as -- in the top left corner.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the difference is between this document -- that M in the top left corner and the others?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can see quite clearly on there that the middle of the M comes down -- is higher in that one document compared to the other three.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender 7212 and 7212A, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering these two documents as one exhibit or as two different, two separate, exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They should be one exhibit, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received with one P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Barr, you were asked to just -- I just want to clarify something with you on the record. When you receive -- in the process of receiving specimens in order to compare it to a questioned document, do you on occasion receive those documents, that is, the specimens, with information about them, such as known samples of handwriting or other documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're told -- since handwriting is a comparative process, in order to say that a specific person has produced the writing that's in dispute, then we need known samples from the person that is suspected of producing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you don't have any, for example, conclusive information that the person -- that a person whose specimens you're provided with actually produced the specimens in question?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you rely on the person or the people who give you that specimen for that representation?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do. We always say that, when we give advice, that if people provide us with specimens, then they have to be provable as specimens, otherwise we're comparing different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So when you make a finding in terms of comparing the specimen to the questioned document, your finding is really an expression between -- of the relationship between whoever produced the specimen and whoever produced the questioned document; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that, again, is entirely dependent upon the information that you're provided with concerning the specimen?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If we were just provided with two documents and weren't told that one was specimen, then we could just say they were or weren't produce by the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Barr. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Now, a question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wonder if you could clarify for me, Dr. Barr, at page 16, lines 8 to 9, you are recorded as having said, "they have to be provable as specimens, otherwise we're confirming [sic] different things." I wonder if you could clarify for me exactly what you mean "provable as specimens." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, if -- handwriting is a comparative process, so we could just compare two documents and say they're by the same person. Generally, if we're working for the Prosecution, they want to know are they produced by the suspect or a specific person, so in those cases, they provide us with specimen writing of that suspect and say, Compare that with the questioned writing to say whether, for example, the suspect produced it. But obviously the only way that we could ever -- we say it's the suspect, but we are relying on the Prosecution producing specimens that are provable as having been written by the suspect. If at some later date for whatever reason the authenticity of those documents as having been written by the suspect is proved not to be true, then our opinion still holds as regards the conclusion. They just can't be linked back, then, to the suspect. So they would still be linked. Say, for example, we'd said, as an example, there was conclusive evidence that the suspect had written them, but then the writing we used as specimen wasn't attributable to the suspect, then the writing would still be conclusive evidence that it was still by the same person, it just wouldn't be by the suspect if his writing was no longer provable as having been produced by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn to commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone again. And may God's will be done in your testimony today, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's stick with P1972. I think that's the last document that was admitted. Where we were comparing two documents with the last three digits of the ERN being 972 and 580, thank you. Thank you. So the ERNs are 0425850 and 0441-0097.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the numbers. Mr. Tolimir wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think General Tolimir is referring to P125 and P520 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see one of them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you see both on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, we have both of them on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that you received a request from Ms. Gallagher electronically to forensically examine these two documents and produce your findings. This is my question: Were you able to receive originals of these documents if the request was sent to you electronically? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received the originals of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why, then, in the report under item 3 that we were looking at here, on page 6 in line 1, you said that you received Erin Gallagher's request in her e-mail dated the 30th November, 2009. So could you have -- and is it possible at all to receive originals of documents by e-mail? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. But I received the request electronically; she asked if we could do it. The documents were sent by courier separately to the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any reference that you could give us, either in your report or otherwise, of your receipt of these documents by a courier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got a copy of the TNT label that we received in my case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see from the TNT label that you received the originals of these documents and not just copies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the courier details it won't tell you that I received the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, is it at all possible to examine documents received by e-mail in order to ascertain all the various particulars such as you've just described for us in relation to the various characters, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, if they had been well scanned and there were obvious differences in the typescript, the typescript that had been used, then, yes, it would be possible. The details that require microscopic examination, it probably wouldn't be possible to do from copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here the two documents for which you concluded that they did not originate from the same machine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move the document to the right slightly so that we can see the date on the left-hand side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you can see, the document was produced on the 13th of July, 1995, as written by hand. At least that's what the date purports to be, because we don't have it typewritten. And you see that the other document was produced on the 5th of July. And you claim that the typewriter wasn't the same in these two instances, and I may agree with you on that. If you bear in mind the fact that the author of the document on the left-hand side did not have his own typewriter but used the machine on which the other one was produced, you claim that they do not come from the same typewriter; the Prosecution knows that the witness did not have a typewriter of his own, that he would use the one on which the document on the right-hand side was typed up on the 5th of July; based on what can we parties to this proceeding know that the document wasn't -- that a document that was sent to you had not actually been typed up on a different typewriter and then sent for you to examine it -- to you to examine it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact this is a very complicated question. I didn't understand the essence of it. But, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask -- well, the first issue is whether or not it properly characterises the testimony to which it refers, and I do not believe that that is the case. If General Tolimir's contention is that the witness stated that he produced a document on the right of the screen using a single typewriter or that there was only one typewriter, I'd like him to provide a reference in the transcript so that at least that's clear for the witness. Other than that, you're right; I think the question is rather inartfully phrased, and I would ask him to phrase it in a manner that's at least understandable to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please rephrase your question in order to enable the witness to provide you with a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Barr, the writer of this text, signed as Milorad -- Colonel Milorad Sacic, he used the typewriter in the headquarters of the brigade which is listed on the right-hand side document, and this in -- and this was only several days apart between the two documents and he didn't have his own typewriter, so is it possible that one of the two documents was typed up on a completely different machine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said that they were typed on different machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my second question: Why do you compare the text which has very few characters or words in common with the other text? Why didn't you ask for identical texts to be sent to you, identical in substance, but produced on different typewriters in order to facilitate your examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Umm, since I've -- since these are typewriters that have fixed, fixed characters, that their -- normally the metal, what we'd call slugs, what the characters actually produced, then I've compared each character in turn between the two documents, so there may not be the words the same but there are the same letters of the alphabet and I've compared each letter that is in common between the two to come to my conclusions. Does that answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please answer this question: Would it have been easier for you to examine the features of these characters had you had two identical samples? For instance, if the two texts on the screen were identical. Perhaps I haven't been clear enough. Would it have suited you better if you had the same sample text as that of the questioned text? Would that have made your analysis easier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Provided -- and I think in, if I check my notes, that I had nearly all the letters of the alphabet on both, it wouldn't have made any difference, specifically because I was asked if these two documents were produced on the same machine, so I'm comparing the documents as opposed to comparing them to a machine, I'm just comparing the documents together. If I'd been asked, This is the machine, does this document come from it? Then, yes, having the same typescript would have helped. But in this particular case, I'm asked to compare these two documents. They have nearly all the characters in common between them, so they were more than suitable for comparison purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do all the characters of the alphabet feature on the text that we see on the right-hand side on our screens?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your examination about these two documents not having been typed up on the same typewriter? Was that what you were examining? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given the four documents and asked, Were they produced on the same machine?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the documents on the screen. These two documents, were they typed on the same typewriter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Prosecution tell you that the signatory -- that the signatories of both these documents typed documents in the same headquarters on the same typewriter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was given any information about the production of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you ask for all the documents available that were typed up on that location, on that particular location, at that particular time to be delivered to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was simply asked about these four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you bearing in mind the question put to you by Her Honour Judge Nyambe when you said that you needed to have a sufficient number of authentic documents in order to infallibly ascertain which of them are genuine and which are not. In other words, did you ask for specimens to be sent to you or did you analyse the specimens that the Prosecution sent you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that Judge Nyambe was asking about specimen handwriting as opposed to typescript, and so that referred to handwriting, needing specimens. For typescript, as I said, if we had been provided -- asked if they were produced on a specific machine, then we would have needed samples from that machine. In this case, I was asked if these four documents were all produced on one machine, and so my comparison can only take place with those four documents, to say whether or not they were produced on the same machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You conducted your expertise based on the items you received. That's sufficient for us at the moment, and we will be looking into this fact whether these persons produced the documents on these machines. I do apologise for the tenor of my questions, but the Defence is really interested in finding out how these documents came into being.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 7212 shown, please. This is your report dated the 8th of January, 2010. And can we show page 3 where it is stated that you received the said documents on the 30th of November, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P1972.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 on the right-hand side, which is what I understand because it's in the Serbian language, or for you it is on the left-hand side, it's stated here that: "I have examined the items listed below at the instruction of Erin Gallagher of the UN ICTY as detailed in her e-mail dated the 30th of November, 2009." It has to do with the same documents we have just discussed. My question is this: The documents you examined, did you receive them by electronic mail and did you carry out your expertise based on copies of these documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received the original documents by courier. And I actually received them on the 10th of December, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: However, you say here that you received an e-mail from Ms. Gallagher. If you cannot produce those documents now before the Court, perhaps you could at least tell us what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the instructions from Ms. Gallagher by e-mail. I received the documents by courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness told that already earlier during your examination, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Ms. Barr. Could we next have 65 ter document 7212A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document was disclosed to us recently. In the list of documents, it is stated that the photographs found in that document are linked to the 8th of January, 2010, report. As we can see, the date on this document is the 15th of March, 2007. My question is this: The document we have on the screen, did it have something to do with the expertise you carried out between the 30th of November, 2009, and the 8th of January, 2010?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of the 15th of March is the date of issue of this document. It's -- part of the quality control system for the company is that this is a digital image examination form, so that date is related to the date of issue of the form rather than the production of the photographs. So the photographs were produced when I had the original documents as part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Did you carry out your expertise only based on these images that we find in the document, or did you also rely on other material?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My examination was based on the original documents and the comparison and examination of the original typed documents. These images were produced as part of my examination as a way of illustrating the differences that I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Barr, can you tell me this: Did you state in your report that these documents were produced on the same typewriter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The images on the screen are all from one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you not state in your report what the typewriter in question is, such as make and model?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was asked if they were produced on one machine, not what make and model of machine it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a possibility that these three documents for which you state were produced on the same typewriter were actually produced on different typewriters of the same make or model, that is to say that the same company manufactured those typewriters and that they were of the same model?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been no damage features and they were simply -- they were all typing perfectly as they were manufactured, then there would be no way of telling. But in this case, we've got features such as the damage to the P which, in my opinion, would not have occurred in exactly the same way on two different machines, which allows me to distinguish between different makes and models of the same machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Prosecutor let you know the year of production, the type of the machine, and other elements that would be interesting for you to know so that you could make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I received no such information from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If two documents are produced on two different typewriters of the same model, is it possible to examine and ascertain on which of the machines the original document that you are examining was produced?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the features of the typewriting that those machines were producing. If, for example, they were two new machines that came straight out of the company boxes and had no unique features, then, no. But once you start using them and they get damaged and they get their own unique identifying characteristics, then, yes, it is possible to determine which machines produced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the typewriters are from the same batch, is there a possibility they will produce the same prints of the letters, given that they were actually produced serially and they were not unique?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the type of damage features here are such that they're not the type that I would expect to see as a manufacturing defect. You've got the -- and also you've got the combination of the damage to the P, the position of the ribbon when the documents are being typed, and the fact that the V is printing; you've got more than one distinguishing feature for these machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Barr. Please tell us this: Can you ascertain the type of the typewriter through your examination since we have a number of witnesses whom we can ask what kind of typewriters they used in order to arrive at a final conclusion as to which typewriter they actually used?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been asked to do that, it may have been possible. It's not something that we do very often now and it would depend on how up-to-date the records of these types of machines were. Theoretically it's possible to identify makes of machine from their typescript within certain caveats in that companies are taken over and therefore more than one company can produce the same type of typescript, and so you need to have very good records or you may not be able to identify it down to one particular make and model.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago we saw two documents for which you ascertained they were not typed on the same typewriter. Is there a possibly that both documents were typed up on an Olympia typewriter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 7212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P1972.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could we have P1972, page 2. It is the report of the 8th of January, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In item 2, you clearly state, and I quote: "I clearly stated which facts and issues in this examination fall within the scope of my expertise and which do not."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have paragraph 2.1 of this document and I will quote from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you say that: "Specialists in questioned documents all have an understanding of issues relating to handwriting and signatures and other aspects of document examination that routinely arise in their field. These include methods of examining documents to show their authenticity or to determine alterations on them -- to them; the examination and comparison of handwritings and signatures and general examinations such as for indented impressions. Beyond this knowledge, practitioners must be aware of their own limitations and have an awareness of the more specialised examination methods other practitioners may be able to offer." My question is this: Do you primarily analyse handwritings or impressions produced by typewriters?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of our work is -- does involve handwriting signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Barr. Can you tell me why in your report in part, titled "Scope of Expertise," you formulated this paragraph so as to conclude that you analysed signatures rather than analysing whether different documents were produced on the same typewriter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this whole part 2 was devised to show that there are some people who look at handwriting signatures, other people who look at the non-handwriting parts of them, and that actually varies across Europe. In England, document examiners look at all aspects of document examination, so that covers both handwriting signatures and the non-handwriting part, such as typewriter examinations, printers, inks, counterfeit documents, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Barr. In order to establish whether documents were produced on the same typewriter, which is something that this Court needs to know, does one need to have further information on the year, model, and make of the typewriter in order to make the job easier for those who are eventually supposed to draw conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since I was simply asked, Were they produced on the same machine, when that machine was produced doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your answer, however, for the needs of these proceedings, it would probably be necessary for us to have the machine itself. Or, if not that, to at least have some more details about the model of the typewriter so that the Court could arrive at relevant conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was actually: Is it necessary when examining documents produced on a typewriter to also have information about the model of the typewriter used in the course of production? Especially it is a matter that needs to be litigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have received an answer to that earlier. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I still haven't received any answer. I may have overlooked it. In any case, I'll move on, as long as you heard the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the witness indicated several times that it was not necessary to know about the model and the machine itself. Only by comparison of the documents she could indicate and distinguish if it was written on the same machine or not. That was the answer we heard several times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the witness is confirming that. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that case, I'd like to ask the witness the following: Can you guarantee that the person forwarding the documents for your examination to you actually forwarded the very documents produced on the particular typewriter? Are you to be held accountable for the veracity of that fact or the person who actually sent you the documents in question?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only compare what I received from the Prosecution. I have no knowledge of where those documents came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Barr. This suffices. My next question is this: On page 3, in paragraph 2.4, I believe we'll see it on the screen shortly, you state: "Some related aspects require expertise in highly specialised fields such as security printing or the detailed analysis of specialised inks or papers. Experts in such areas may not necessarily have a detailed knowledge of the other aspects of questioned documents but will often work in partnership with other document examiners to ensure that all aspects of the task are correctly addressed." My question is this. In your report you state your opinion about the degree of certainty that the two documents in question, which is 0425850 and 044100972 [as interpreted], were produced on the same typewriter. In relation to that, I'd like to ask you this: Is it necessary to have all the elements you refer to in paragraph 2.4 in order to draw such conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.4 refers to the fact that there are experts that work with banks, for example, who only have knowledge of printing of bank notes, so they are an expert in that area not in any other area, and so for cases involving bank notes they should work in conjunction with other document examiners to ensure that what has been asked, whatever that might be, is answered. So it doesn't really refer to my comparison of the typewritten documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Barr. In your report in paragraph 5.3, which we are about to see, you state that the lower-case letter P on these documents has a slight damage to the left-hand side of the bottom horizontal line. My question is this: Since you used the term slight damage or partial damage to the bottom line, are you trying to point out that there was a particular feature on the slug for the production of the letter P, or are you actually referring to something else? Was there a defect?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to a defect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What may have been the reason for that defect to occur, the mere use of the machine or any particular mechanical feature of the typewriter? Was it due to wear and tear or something else? Can you tell us what the basic cause may have been?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this particular machine, I don't -- wouldn't know the cause, but generally the defects I've encountered in these types of typewriters is normally caused by wear and tear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Such defects, can they also occur during production itself? And is it possible that all typewriters of the same batch have the same defect? Is there such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do all typewriters have -- make different prints irrespective of the model match as would be the case with finger-prints?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typewriters have a fixed each -- they have a fixed typestyle that's produced by the manufacturer and how the slugs have been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If possible, please answer this, since we are not experts in this field, can you explain it in lay terms: Is there a possibility that all typewriters of the same model have different prints or produce different prints which occur between the time of production and the end of their life much as would be the case with regular finger-prints and dermal ridges?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typewriters, when they're produced, of the same model would produce the same print. But as they wear over time, then they can develop their own unique features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our first break. You may continue after the break. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's take it up from where we left off. You say that the machines wear over time and they develop peculiar features. My question is this: Does the position of the machine at the time it is being used have any bearing on the eventual peculiar features it may develop in the prints? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may do if it was exposed to more things that are likely to damage it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. May an inadequate bearing, or underneath a typewriter, for instance, if it's placed on an inadequate surface, have any impact on the possible defects that may develop in the prints? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the specimens you examined, in addition to the damage to the Ps and Vs, you also observed a difference in colouration. My question is this: Can the use of different ribbons on the same typewriter produce different prints, although the text was produced on the same machine? Because normally where you have different ribbons, this would have an impact on the text printed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't affect the style of the text, though it may affect the colour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it affect the degree to which the characters are filled in, for instance, in the case of the letters V and P? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By filled in, I was referring to dirt on the actual -- the characters. That was meaning that it was -- more was being transferred onto the paper. So to that extent, no, the ribbon wouldn't affect that. It would affect the amount that you could see. Again, if you had a newer ribbon with more ink in it, then the print would be darker and you would see darker filling in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I ask this because in the texts you use as referential originals we were able to see different impressions of characters which seemed quite faded. You are a forensic document examiner. This is my question: Were you asked to determine the degree of certainty that the documents you examined were produced at a time at which they were purported to have been produced? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you able to establish the time when a document came into being based on the typewritten impressions you were given for forensic examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was simply asked to compare the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your position. Can experts establish the time when a document was produced and which was typed up on a specific typewriter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the time when a document was produced, no. Whether it was typed on a specific typewriter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible for any expert to determine the time when a document was produced? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what document. Dating documents is a very specialised and difficult field. As regards typewriting, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what sort of forensic examination is required in order to establish the time when a typewritten document was produced? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of any means of determining when a typewritten document was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the chemical substance of the impressions, that's to say of the text itself, contribute to this process? Do they affect the process in any way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may do. As I say, to the best of my knowledge, for typescript, I don't think it's possible. For example, there are still old-fashioned typewriters and ribbons dating back many years that people still have, so it would still be possible to produce something today that was produced on an old-style typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe my question wasn't clear enough. Let me give you an illustration. The Prosecution here challenged the time when certain entries were made, altered, or erased. We as the Defence also challenge the origin of certain documents, whether they are of pre-war or post-war origin. Can you tell us, what are the features that can determine the time of origin of a document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the specific document that you were talking about. So, for example, if you were talking pre-Second World War, you wouldn't expect to see ball-point pen on it, so that's one way of dating documents. As regards, as I say, typescript, I'm not aware of any means of determining when it was produced. There are some -- in the UK it's not something that is done routinely. Dating of documents, there is a lot of research being done in America on dating handwritten documents by dating the alterations in inks, but it's not very reliable at the moment. And as I say, for typewritten documents I don't think it's possible, or I'm not aware of any means of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you forensically examined handwritten texts for the purposes of this trial, this is my question: Based on the examination of the date when a paper was manufactured or on the pen impressions, is it possible to establish -- or to date the documents that were the subject of your forensic examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it would depend on a lot of other factors. For example, you would have to know when the paper was manufactured, and in effect all that could tell you was, if you knew that precisely, that the document couldn't have been produced prior to that date, but it couldn't tell you after that date when it had been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the chemical substance of the ink or any other matter used to produce the impression point to the date when the document was produced?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I think there is some research that says that you can date documents by how the ink has changed over time. As far as I am aware, I don't know the time, how closely you could differentiate, I suspect in terms of years it may be possible, providing you're looking at the same ink on the same piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, on page 6 of today's transcript, in line 6, you spoke of -- or actually, it's paragraph 6 of your report, I'm sorry. You say that there are some features in the questioned text which are not consistent with the signature specimen. And at page 78 of the transcript, that's the extent of what you said in answer to the Prosecutor's questions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not entirely sure to what you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 75 you spoke about the contents of the document written by Dragan Jokic. You went on to speak about your findings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then I asked you on page 78 -- or, rather, the Prosecutor asked you about Vujadin Popovic's signature, and then at paragraph 6.5 you speak of the questioned signature, and then at item 6.6 of your report you say that some of the features in the questioned text are not consistent with the signature specimen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the relevant portion shown on the screen in order for you to see the point I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it will come up very soon. You were referring to the transcript -- just to clarify, you were referring to the transcript of yesterday during the cross-examination of Mr. -- examination-in-chief of Mr. Vanderpuye; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was referring to the examination of today. I was referring to pages 77 and 78. I'm not sure where exactly the reference can be found. Yesterday, I believe that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Yesterday, not today. We don't have -- reached the page 78 today. We need paragraph 6.6 on the screen of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'm referring to P1969, but I'm not sure that my notes are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I'm confused. We had the document P1972 on the screen. You -- and I don't know which document you want to have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have now P1969 on the screen I was told.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at item 6.6 if we have it. If we don't, can we then look at P1969. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is on the screen. Paragraph 6.6 can't be found in this document. You should check it again. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I think the reference that General Tolimir is talking about, referring to paragraph 6.6, is from a different document which is P1967, but that document refers to Drago Nikolic and not Vujadin Popovic, so it's unclear whether General Tolimir is referring to Drago Nikolic or Vujadin Popovic for the purposes of the question he wishes to put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I meant Drago Nikolic, since that's what the expert referred to. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Can we have P1967. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now tell us, please, the page number and/or the paragraph number. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On my feet again, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 1968, not 1967. I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then move to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the paragraph 6.6 on the screen. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just read it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I was looking for cannot be found under 6.6. But under 6.7, in line 4, it reads: "However, there are some features of the construction and proportions of these questioned signatures that are less well matched. While these differences may be due to the small size of the signature boxes, they have prevented me from expressing any strong opinion. Nevertheless, the similarities do, in my opinion, provide some limited evidence that Drago Nikolic produced the specified signatures on the vehicle log" of such and such a number. "However, the possibility of simulation cannot be ruled out." Thank you. That's the relevant part I was looking for, which was in paragraph 6.7 rather than 6.6 so I apologise to everyone. Can this provide conclusive evidence that Drago Nikolic made the entry himself or that somebody made the entry in his stead? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It provides limited evidence that Drago Nikolic produced the signatures, but I can't exclude the fact that somebody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You are a doctor of sciences and you received your doctorate in plant pathology. Can you tell us briefly what sort of scientific field this is and in what way it is related to your forensic expertise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to do with a virus relating to sugar beet, so it has absolutely no relevance to my expertise in forensic science, other than it being a scientific degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've just told us that you received your doctorate in this field, is it possible to decry traces invisible to the naked eye by dowsing the paper with a certain substance which would enable us to see if the entry made on that piece of paper is identical to the rest of the text contained on that sheet of paper? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question. Do you mean identical to the ink or identical to the writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll repeat my question. If we have a set of writing where an alteration was made of several words or a single word, is it possible by analysing invisible features of the chemical impression of the various characters and the rest of the text to ascertain that there are differences between the different sets of writings on the piece of paper if -- and that by adding some substance to it, such as smearing it with a citric acid or something of the sort? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the -- adding some substance. It would be possible to analyse the inks to determine if they were different, which may indicate that a different pen had been used, which, depending on the circumstances, may indicate an alteration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. In addition to the forensic examination of documents and in particular handwriting, do you also work in the other scientific field within which you received your doctorate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've been a forensic document examiner since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you understand the Serbian language used in the documents you examined for the purposes of this Tribunal and testimony?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to analyse a handwriting, is it necessary to be acquainted with the elements of the language and script used in the document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no, provided that you can identify the individual characters to make sure that you're comparing like with like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this in keeping with certain general guide-lines that graphologists have to abide by when analysing documents and handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Therefore, I can conclude that such an examination meets the standard threshold required of any graphologist when carrying out an analysis of a particular handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The examination that I carried out here, yes, meets the standard that we would do for all our examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that it does meet the standard, my question is this: Does it make it more difficult for the forensic examiner in question to examine a certain document without being familiar with the language and script used in the document that is being examined?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It takes more preparation to be certain that you're comparing like with like. Once that process has been taken into account, then we would use the same principles that we used -- or I would use in comparing writing in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that, for the purposes of your examination as you were tasked by the OTP, you analysed a large number of documents that were created either on typewriters or by writing, did you use the assistance of anyone familiar with the Serbian language and script during your examination?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Other than I had -- I was provided with transliterations of certain parts of the writing to enable me to identify the characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who carried out these transliterations?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN BARR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that you don't know, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you answer this question? You were asked: "Can you tell us who carried out these transliterations?" And you said, "No." Does it mean you don't know or are there other reasons why you can't tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I only got up to the "or." I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to thank the witness as well, our expert witness, Ms. Kathryn Barr, for her assistance and clarifications that serve our needs. Thank you for being here, and thank you for this opportunity to put questions to you since we are unfamiliar with the topic as laypersons. I'd like to thank you on behalf of the Defence. I wish you a safe journey back home. And may God bless you in your further activities. Thank you yet again. Thank you, Mr. President. This concludes the Defence examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, well, just two things. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Enjoy your -- the remainder of your working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Thayer is taking the next witness. Good afternoon, Mr. Thayer. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
